  • Bleeding genital ulcer 
  • Painful lymph node

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Treponema pallidum: This is the causative agent of syphilis, which typically presents with a painless genital ulcer called a chancre and painless lymphadenopathy during the primary stage.

 

Option C. Calymmatobacterium (Klebsiella granulomatis): This organism causes granuloma inguinale (donovanosis), which presents with painless ulcers that progressively spread, and the lymph nodes are usually not significantly enlarged or tender.

 

Option D. Herpes: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) causes painful genital ulcers, but the associated lymphadenopathy is typically non-tender. The ulcers in herpes are multiple, grouped vesicles that rupture to form painful erosions.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A painful genital ulcer accompanied by painful, soft, non-indurated inguinal lymph nodes suggests chancroid, which is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. Recognizing the key features helps in differentiating it from other sexually transmitted infections like syphilis, donovanosis, and herpes.

questions.stem: Swarming is seen in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Clostridium tetani

 

Swarming is a characteristic movement of certain bacteria on agar plates, where they rapidly spread across the surface, creating waves or concentric rings. This is seen in Clostridium tetani, as well as other bacteria such as Proteus species and Bacillus cereus. When these bacteria are inoculated at the center of an agar plate, they start moving outward rapidly, producing a wavy pattern, which is referred to as swarming.

 

Note:

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Clostridium perfringens: Clostridium perfringens is non motile, it typically does not exhibit a pronounced swarming motility. Instead, it forms characteristic "double-zone" hemolysis on blood agar due to its exotoxins.

 

Option C. Clostridium botulinum: Clostridium botulinum is motile, but it does not display swarming growth. Its primary pathogenicity is related to the production of botulinum toxin, which causes flaccid paralysis.

 

Option D. Clostridium difficile: Clostridium difficile is also motile, but its colonies do not show swarming motility. Its pathogenicity is due to the production of toxins A and B, which lead to colonic inflammation and pseudomembranous colitis.

 

Educational objective:

 

Clostridium tetani exhibits swarming on agar plates, alongside other bacteria like Proteus and Bacillus cereus.

questions.stemHtml: Which is the mode of transmission and infective form of the parasite whose egg picture is given below?

options.label: B
options.text: Ingestion of egg contaminated in water

questions.answerText: Ingestion of egg contaminated in water
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Ingestion of egg contaminated in water

 

The image shows the egg of Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), which is characterized by its barrel-shaped structure and mucus plugs at both poles. This egg is bile stained, indicating that it is passed through feces. 

 

 

The mode of transmission of Trichuris trichiura is by ingesting the egg contaminated in water or food. The eggs hatch in the small intestine, and the larvae migrate to the large intestine, where they mature into adult worms.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ingestion of uncooked/raw beef: Incorrect. This is related to Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm), not Trichuris trichiura.

 

Option C. Penetration by filariform larva: Incorrect. This is related to Strongyloides stercoralis and Ancylostoma species (hookworms), which penetrate through the skin.

 

Option D. Penetration by rhabditiform larva: Incorrect. This also applies to the life cycle of Strongyloides stercoralis, not Trichuris trichiura.

 

Educational objective:

 

The key identifiers for Trichuris trichiura eggs are the barrel shape with mucus plugs at the poles, and the transmission is through ingestion of eggs contaminated in water or food.

questions.stem: A child with bull neck and membrane over tonsil. What is the mechanism of the toxin responsible for this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Inhibits Elongation Factor-2

 

This presentation of bull neck and a membrane over the tonsil is suggestive of diphtheria, which is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae. The key mechanism of the diphtheria toxin is the inhibition of elongation factor-2 (EF-2). This inhibition leads to the blockage of protein synthesis by halting the elongation step of translation, ultimately preventing ribosome function and causing cell death.

 

Note:

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Increased cAMP: While some bacterial toxins (such as cholera toxin) work by increasing cyclic AMP levels, this is not the mechanism for the diphtheria toxin.

 

Option B. Inhibits GABA neurons: This is the mechanism of action for tetanus toxin, not diphtheria toxin.

 

Option D. Inhibits release of acetylcholine: This is the mechanism of botulinum toxin, which affects neuromuscular transmission, not diphtheria.

 

Educational objective:

 

The diphtheria toxin works by inhibiting elongation factor-2 (EF-2), blocking protein synthesis and leading to cell death. This is the cause of the severe symptoms seen in diphtheria, such as the bull neck and membrane over the tonsils.

questions.stem: In HIV, the window period indicates:

options.label: A
options.text: Time period between infection and onset of first symptoms

options.label: B
options.text: Time period between infection and detection of antibodies against HIV

options.label: C
options.text: Time period between infection and minimum multiplication of the organism

options.label: D
options.text: Time period between infection and maximum multiplication of the organism

questions.answerText: Time period between infection and detection of antibodies against HIV
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Time period between infection and detection of antibodies against HIV

 

The window period in HIV refers to the time between initial infection and when antibodies against HIV become detectable in the blood through standard tests like ELISA. During this period, the infected individual is highly infectious, as the HIV virus is present in the bloodstream, but antibodies have not yet reached detectable levels. This period typically lasts 2-8 weeks but can extend up to a few months. During this time, tests that rely solely on antibody detection may produce false-negative results. However, HIV can be detected during the window period using other methods, such as the p24 antigen assay or PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Time period between infection and onset of first symptoms: This describes the incubation period, not the window period. The incubation period refers to the time between infection and the appearance of clinical symptoms.

 

Option C. Time period between infection and minimum multiplication of the organism: This Option D. oes not accurately describe the window period. The window period is not defined by the multiplication rate of the virus but by the lack of detectable antibodies.

 

Option D. Time period between infection and maximum multiplication of the organism: Similar to option (c), this is not a correct description of the window period. The window period is concerned with the gap between infection and antibody detection.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The HIV window period is the time between infection and when antibodies become detectable. During this period, the person is highly infectious, but standard antibody tests may not yet show a positive result.

questions.stemHtml: A patient has painful tiny vesicular ulcers on the lips. A Tzanck smear was made from the scraping of the lesion. Identify the pathogen:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Herpes simplex

 

The Tzanck smear is a diagnostic test commonly used for detecting herpes virus infections, including Herpes simplex virus (HSV). The presence of multinucleated giant cells on a Tzanck smear, as seen in the image, is characteristic of herpes infections.

 

Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) is the most likely cause of painful vesicular lesions on the lips, a condition known as herpes labialis. HSV-1 is typically responsible for infections above the waist, including cold sores and oral herpes, while HSV-2 is more commonly associated with genital infections. However, both types can show similar findings on a Tzanck smear.

 

Cutaneous lesions

 

HSV-1 usually produces lesions above the waist

HSV-2 usually produces lesions below the waist

 

 

HSV-1 → Orofacialmucosal lesions

 

 

  • Most common manifestations

 

 

  • Most common affected site → buccal mucosa

 

 

  • Most frequent recurrent lesion → herpes labialis (painful vesicles near lips)

 

HSV – 2 → Genital lesions

 

 

  • Bilateral, painful multiple, tiny vesicular ulcers
  • Associates with fever and inguinal lymphadenopathy

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Varicella zoster: While Varicella zoster (the cause of chickenpox and shingles) can also produce vesicular lesions and show multinucleated giant cells on a Tzanck smear, it typically presents with a more widespread rash rather than localized lip ulcers.

 

Option C. Parvovirus: Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) and is not associated with vesicular lesions or multinucleated giant cells.

 

Option D. HPV (Human Papillomavirus): HPV causes warts but does not produce vesicular lesions or multinucleated giant cells. Its diagnosis is usually made through other means like biopsy and histology.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) is the most common cause of painful vesicular ulcers on the lips, and a Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells is a key diagnostic finding.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man underwent kidney transplantation. Two months after transplantation, he developed fever and features suggestive of bilateral diffuse interstitial pneumonitis. Which of the following is the most likely etiologic agent?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Cytomegalovirus

 

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the most common viral cause of pneumonia in immunocompromised individuals, including organ transplant recipients. CMV infection typically manifests 1 to 4 months post-transplant due to reactivation of latent infection or through donor transmission. In this case, the patient developed fever and interstitial pneumonitis, which is a hallmark presentation of CMV infection in transplant recipients.

 

CMV can also cause systemic effects, such as leukopenia, gastrointestinal inflammation, and hepatitis, further complicating recovery post-transplant. Early diagnosis and management with antiviral agents like ganciclovir are crucial to prevent severe complications.

 

Persons at greatest risk for cytomegalovirus disease are

 

  • Those receiving organ transplants (Kidney or solid organs),
  • Those with malignant tumors who are receiving chemotherapy, and
  • Those with AIDS.
  • Viral excretion is increased and prolonged, and the infection is more apt to become disseminated.

 

Diffuse Interstitial Pneumonia is the most common complication

However, it is less commonly associated with diffuse interstitial pneumonitis in post-transplant patients. HSV more often causes localized mucocutaneous infections and encephalitis in such patients.

 

Option C. Epstein-Barr virus: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is known for causing post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders (PTLD) rather than pulmonary complications like interstitial pneumonitis. While EBV can reactivate in immunocompromised individuals, it is not the typical cause of pneumonia in post-kidney transplant patients.

 

Option D. Varicella Zoster virus: Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV) can cause severe infections in immunocompromised individuals, including disseminated infections and pneumonia. However, it is not as common a cause of diffuse interstitial pneumonitis in the post-transplant setting as CMV. VZV more typically presents with skin lesions or shingles in this population.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cytomegalovirus is a common cause of diffuse interstitial pneumonitis in post-transplant patients, particularly within the first few months following transplantation due to their immunocompromised state.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old child presents with fever and cervical lymphadenopathy. Oral examination shows a grey membrane on the right tonsil extending to the anterior pillar. Which of the following medium will be ideal for the culture of the throat swab for a rapid identification of the pathogen?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Loffler’s serum slope

 

The clinical presentation of fever, cervical lymphadenopathy, and a grey pseudomembrane on the tonsils strongly suggests an infection with Corynebacterium diphtheriae, the causative agent of diphtheria.

 

For rapid identification of C. diphtheriae, the best medium to use is Loffler’s serum slope, as it facilitates the development of the metachromatic granules of C. diphtheriae within 6–8 hours. The medium is enriched with serum, which enhances the growth and identification of this organism.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Nutrient agar: This is a general-purpose medium and is not selective for C. diphtheriae.

 

Option B. Blood agar: Though enriched, it is not the most ideal for the rapid detection of C. diphtheriae.

 

Option D. Lowenstein-Jensen medium: This medium is used for culturing Mycobacterium tuberculosis, not C. diphtheriae.

 

 

Educational objective:

 

For the rapid identification of Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Loffler’s serum slope is the preferred medium, as it enhances the development of characteristic metachromatic granules within 6–8 hours.

questions.stem: A vitreous aspirate from a case of metastatic endophthalmitis on culture yields Gram-positive round to oval cells, 12-14 μm in size. The aspirate on Gram staining shows the presence of pseudohyphae. Which of the following is the most likely etiological agent?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Candida

 

The presence of Gram-positive round to oval yeast cells measuring 12-14 μm with pseudohyphae in a vitreous aspirate is characteristic of Candida species. Candida is a yeast that can form pseudohyphae, which are elongated yeast cells that remain attached after division, appearing as chains. These features are crucial for distinguishing Candida from other fungi.

 

In cases of metastatic endophthalmitis, Candida can disseminate from a systemic infection and establish an infection in the eye, leading to inflammation within the eye (endophthalmitis). This is a common occurrence in immunocompromised individuals or patients with prolonged hospitalization.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Aspergillus: Aspergillus is a mold and appears as septate hyphae rather than pseudohyphae or yeast forms. It does not match the description of round to oval cells seen in the aspirate.

 

Option B. Rhizopus: Rhizopus is a mold from the Mucorales group and forms broad, ribbon-like non-septate hyphae. It does not produce yeast cells or pseudohyphae.

 

Option D. Fusarium: Fusarium is a mold known for its filamentous growth, producing septate hyphae and characteristic conidia (spores). It does not produce yeast cells or pseudohyphae, making it an incorrect choice here.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of pseudohyphae with round to oval yeast cells in a Gram-positive fungal culture suggests an infection by Candida species, which can cause metastatic endophthalmitis in immunocompromised individuals.

questions.stem: A rose gardener has multiple vesicles on hand and multiple eruptions along the lymphatics. Most common fungus responsible is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Sporothrix schenckii

 

The scenario of a rose gardener with multiple vesicles on the hand and eruptions along the lymphatics is a classic presentation of Sporotrichosis, caused by the fungus Sporothrix schenckii. This thermally dimorphic fungus is introduced into the skin via trauma, such as a thorn prick injury, which is common among gardeners, hence the name "Rose Gardener’s Disease." The infection spreads along the lymphatic channels, causing multiple ulcers or vesicles along the lymphatic drainage path, a hallmark of Sporotrichosis.

 

 

  • On biopsy, characteristic star-shaped bodies (also known as asteroid bodies or cigar bodies) are observed.
  • The presence of these star-shaped structures is a hallmark diagnostic feature of sporotrichosis.

 

 

Note:

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Cladosporium: This is incorrect because Cladosporium is not typically associated with this clinical presentation. It is a mold that can cause allergic reactions but does not usually cause lymphatic spread of vesicles.

 

Option C. Histoplasma: This is incorrect because Histoplasma is more commonly associated with pulmonary infections and does not present with lymphatic vesicles or ulcers along the lymphatics.

 

Option D. Candida: This is incorrect because Candida usually causes superficial or mucosal infections, not the type of lymphatic spread seen in Sporotrichosis.

 

Educational objective:

 

Sporotrichosis, caused by Sporothrix schenckii, is characterized by ulcers and vesicles along the lymphatics following a thorn prick injury, commonly seen in rose gardeners.

questions.stem: The following is false about Adenovirus:

options.label: C
options.text: Hemorrhagic cystitis is due to type 11,21

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) SSDNA virus

 

Adenovirus is a double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) virus, not a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) virus. This makes option (a) incorrect. Adenoviruses belong to a family of viruses that contain linear, double-stranded DNA and have an icosahedral capsid. The only DNA virus that is single-stranded is Parvovirus. Therefore, describing adenovirus as an ssDNA virus is false.

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Icosahedral: This is true. Adenoviruses have an icosahedral capsid structure, which is common among many DNA viruses.

 

Option C. Hemorrhagic cystitis is due to type 11, 21: This is correct. Adenovirus types 11 and 21 are known to cause hemorrhagic cystitis, particularly in children and immunocompromised individuals.

 

Option D. Diarrheagenic is due to type 40: This statement is true. Adenovirus types 40 and 41 are associated with gastrointestinal infections and can cause diarrhea, especially in infants and young children.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Adenovirus is a double-stranded DNA virus, not a single-stranded DNA virus. Remember, only Parvovirus among DNA viruses is single-stranded.

questions.stem: A patient was presented to the hospital with severe hydrophobia. Corneal scrapings from the patient are obtained. What test should be done on this specimen for a diagnosis of Rabies?

options.label: C
options.text: Antibodies to rabies virus by Indirect Immunofluorescence

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) RT-PCR for Rabies virus

 

The patient presents with severe hydrophobia, a hallmark symptom of rabies. Corneal scrapings are collected from the patient for testing, and the most appropriate diagnostic test for rabies in live patients is RT-PCR or antigen detection by direct immunofluorescence (IF).

 

RT-PCR is preferred as it detects the genetic material of the rabies virus directly from the corneal sample. This test is sensitive and can diagnose rabies during the course of infection.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Negri bodies: Incorrect because Negri bodies are inclusion bodies seen in the brain (specifically in the cerebellum and hippocampus) during autopsy, not in corneal scrapings. Therefore, Negri bodies can only be detected after death, making this option incorrect for live patients.

 

Option C. Antibodies to rabies virus by Indirect Immunofluorescence: Incorrect because this test is done on blood samples, not corneal scrapings.

 

Option D. Tzanck smear: Incorrect because this test is used for diagnosing herpes virus infections, not rabies.

 

Educational objective:

 

For diagnosing rabies in live patients using corneal scrapings, RT-PCR is the preferred method, while Negri bodies are only seen in postmortem brain tissue.

questions.stemHtml: The following lesions were seen in a child. The patient is suffering from a disease caused by which of these viruses?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Coxsackie A virus

 

The images show typical lesions seen in Hand-Foot-Mouth Disease (HFMD). HFMD is caused by Coxsackie A virus, specifically Coxsackie A16 in most cases. This viral infection is characterized by:

 

Vesicular rashes on the palms, soles, and oral mucosa.

 

Oral and pharyngeal ulcerations, which are typical signs of HFMD.

 

Coxsackie A virus is an enterovirus and is part of the Picornaviridae family, not the Poxviridae family as sometimes confused. The disease primarily affects young children and is self-limiting.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Pox virus: Incorrect. Poxviruses are known for causing conditions like smallpox and molluscum contagiosum, which do not present with the hand, foot, and mouth rash pattern.

 

Option C. Herpes simplex type 1 virus: Incorrect. Herpes simplex type 1 usually causes cold sores or herpetic gingivostomatitis, but it does not cause the characteristic hand and foot lesions seen in HFMD.

 

Option D. Toga virus: Incorrect. Togaviruses cause diseases like rubella, which presents with a different rash pattern, not the hand-foot-mouth distribution seen in HFMD.

 

Educational objective:

 

Hand-Foot-Mouth Disease is primarily caused by Coxsackie A virus, presenting with oral ulcerations and vesicular rashes on the hands and feet.

questions.stem: Which is the first antibody synthesized in fetal life?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) IgM

 

The first antibody synthesized by the fetus is IgM. Around the 20th week of gestation, the fetus begins to produce its own antibodies, and the first of these is IgM. Although IgG is present in the fetus earlier, it is not synthesized by the fetus itself. IgG is transferred from the mother to the fetus via the placenta. This makes IgG the first antibody found in the fetus, but the first antibody synthesized by the fetus is IgM.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. IgA: IgA is an important antibody for mucosal immunity, but it is not the first antibody produced by the fetus.

 

Option C. IgG: While IgG is present in the fetus, it is transferred from the mother across the placenta. It is not synthesized by the fetus itself, making this option incorrect in the context of fetal synthesis.

 

Option D. IgE: IgE is involved in allergic reactions and parasitic infections, but it is not the first antibody produced by the fetus.

 

Educational objective:

 

The first antibody synthesized by the fetus is IgM, while IgG is the only antibody that crosses the placenta from the mother to the fetus.

questions.stem: Wood’s Lamp is used in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Pityriasis versicolor

 

A Wood’s lamp emits ultraviolet (UV) light, which can detect fluorescence in certain skin conditions and infections. When used on Pityriasis versicolor (also known as Tinea versicolor), caused by the fungus Malassezia, it produces a characteristic yellow-green fluorescence under UV light. This fluorescence helps in the diagnosis of the infection, making Wood’s lamp a useful tool for identifying this condition.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Candida: Candida infections do not typically show fluorescence under a Wood’s lamp, so this test is not used for its diagnosis.

 

Option C. Sporotrichosis: Sporothrix schenckii, the fungus responsible for sporotrichosis, does not fluoresce under Wood’s lamp light.

 

Option D. Histoplasma: Histoplasma capsulatum also does not fluoresce under Wood’s lamp light, so this tool is not useful for its identification.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Wood’s lamp is particularly helpful in diagnosing Pityriasis versicolor, as the affected skin shows a yellow-green fluorescence under UV light, aiding in the identification of this fungal infection.

questions.stem: A patient admitted to an ICU is on central venous line for the last one week. He is on ceftazidime and amikacin. After 7 days of antibiotics, he develops a spike of fever and his blood culture is positive for gram positive cocci in chains, which are catalase negative. Following this, vancomycin was started but the culture remained positive for the same organism even after 2 weeks of therapy. The most likely organism causing infection is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Enterococcus faecalis

 

This is a case of vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) infection. The patient was admitted to the ICU, and after 7 days of being on antibiotics, he developed a spike in fever, which suggests a nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infection. The blood culture showed gram-positive cocci in chains that were catalase-negative, which points to the Streptococcaceae family. Enterococcus faecalis is part of this family and is known to be resistant to aminoglycosides, cephalosporins, and vancomycin.

 

The patient remained culture-positive even after starting vancomycin strongly suggests a multi-drug resistant organism, which is characteristic of Enterococcus faecalis, particularly vancomycin-resistant strains (VRE). 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Staphylococcus aureus: This is incorrect because S. aureus is catalase-positive.

 

Option B. Viridans streptococci: This is incorrect because Viridans streptococci are typically associated with dental infections and endocarditis and do not show this degree of antibiotic resistance.

 

Option D. Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus: This is incorrect because coagulase-negative staphylococci are catalase-positive.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Enterococcus faecalis, especially vancomycin-resistant strains (VRE), are known to cause nosocomial infections, particularly in ICU settings, and show resistance to multiple antibiotics, including vancomycin.

questions.stem: Resistance to HIV infection occurs due to mutation of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) CCR 5

 

Resistance to HIV infection can occur due to a mutation in the CCR5 receptor, known as the CCR5-delta 32 mutation. CCR5 is a coreceptor for the HIV virus found on human macrophages, dendritic cells, and other immune cells. The mutation blocks the entry of HIV into these cells by preventing the virus from fusing with the cell membrane, thus stopping infection. Individuals with this mutation, especially those who are homozygous for the CCR5-delta 32 gene, are highly resistant to HIV infection and do not develop AIDS.

 

 

This mutation is found mainly among Northern Europeans, with approximately 1% of Swedes being homozygous, making them completely resistant to HIV infection. Heterozygous individuals, who inherit one copy of the mutated gene, have a reduced risk of HIV infection and slower progression to AIDS if infected. This mutation is rare or absent in populations such as Africans, East Asians, and Amerindians.

 

Note: 

 

Main receptor: CD4 (present on CD4 lymphocytes and macrophages) binds to GP120 of HIV for attachment.

 

Co-receptor:

 

  • CXCR4 for T lymphocytes.
  • CCR5 for macrophages.

 

GP41 of HIV binds to the co-receptor for fusion.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. CXCR4: This coreceptor is also used by HIV, particularly for infection of T-lymphocytes, but mutations in CXCR4 do not confer resistance to HIV in the way that CCR5 mutations do.

 

Option C. gp41: This is a glycoprotein on the HIV virus that is involved in fusion, but mutations in gp41 do not provide resistance to HIV.

 

Option D. CD4: This is the primary receptor that gp120 of HIV binds to for attachment, but mutations in CD4 do not result in HIV resistance.

 

Educational objective:

 

Resistance to HIV infection is conferred by the CCR5-delta 32 mutation, which blocks the fusion process and prevents the virus from entering immune cells like macrophages.

questions.stem: A chronic alcoholic patient is presented with necrotic pneumonia. Sputum culture reveals mucoid lactose fermenting colonies on MacConkey medium. What is the organism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Klebsiella

 

The presentation of a chronic alcoholic patient with necrotic pneumonia and the identification of mucoid lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar suggests Klebsiella species as the causative agent. Klebsiella pneumoniae is known for producing characteristic mucoid (sticky) colonies due to its polysaccharide capsule. The capsule not only gives the colonies a sticky appearance but also contributes to the virulence of Klebsiella, making it a common cause of pneumonia, particularly in individuals with underlying conditions such as alcoholism.

 

On MacConkey agar, lactose fermenters produce pink colonies due to acid production, and Klebsiella typically forms highly mucoid, pink colonies. This distinguishes it from other lactose fermenters like E. coli, which produces pink colonies but lacks the mucoid, sticky appearance.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. E. coli: While E. coli is also a lactose fermenter and can produce pink colonies on MacConkey agar, it does not typically cause necrotic pneumonia and lacks the distinctive mucoid (sticky) appearance seen with Klebsiella.

 

Option C. Moraxella catarrhalis: This organism is not a lactose fermenter and would not produce pink colonies on MacConkey agar. It is more commonly associated with respiratory infections like otitis media and bronchitis rather than necrotic pneumonia.

 

Option D. Burkholderia: Burkholderia species are generally non-lactose fermenters and would not produce the pink, mucoid colonies observed in this case. They are also less commonly associated with necrotic pneumonia in chronic alcoholics.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Mucoid, lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar, especially in the context of pneumonia in a chronic alcoholic, are strongly indicative of Klebsiella pneumoniae.

questions.stem: Winter bottom sign is seen in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) African trypanosomiasis

 

Winterbottom sign refers to posterior cervical lymphadenopathy (enlarged lymph nodes at the back of the neck) and is a characteristic feature of West African trypanosomiasis, also known as African sleeping sickness. This condition is caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense, a parasite transmitted by the tsetse fly (Glossina species). The sign occurs during the early stages of infection when the parasite spreads to the lymphatic system, leading to swollen lymph nodes in the posterior cervical region.

Other Options:

 

Option B. Toxocariasis: This is caused by Toxocara species, a parasitic infection acquired through soil contaminated with the eggs of the parasite. It does not present with the characteristic posterior cervical lymphadenopathy known as Winterbottom sign.

 

Option C. Leishmaniasis: This disease is caused by Leishmania species and is transmitted by sandflies. It typically presents with skin lesions (cutaneous leishmaniasis) or affects internal organs (visceral leishmaniasis), but not with Winterbottom sign.

 

Option D. Toxoplasmosis: This is caused by Toxoplasma gondii and can present with various symptoms, especially in immunocompromised individuals or during pregnancy. However, it is not associated with the characteristic posterior cervical lymphadenopathy of Winterbottom sign.

 

Educational Objective:

Educational Objective: Winterbottom sign (posterior cervical lymphadenopathy) is a clinical feature specific to West African trypanosomiasis, caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense.

questions.stem: Neonates have hepatosplenomegaly. His urine was stained with Giemsa stain which revealed owl’s eye appearance inclusions. Which will be the most probable cause?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) CMV

 

Neonate with hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. The urine was stained with Giemsa stain, revealing owl eye appearance inclusion bodies. The biggest clue here is the owl eye appearance inclusion bodies, which are a characteristic finding in Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infections. In this case, we are discussing congenital CMV, as it affects a newborn. Congenital CMV can cause microencephaly, micro calcifications in the brain, and hepatosplenomegaly.

 

The owl eye appearance is a typical feature seen in CMV infections. In CMV infections, inclusion bodies can be found in both the nucleus and the cytoplasm, giving them an appearance similar to owl’s eyes.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. HIV: This is incorrect because HIV does not show owl eye appearance inclusion bodies in stained urine, which are specific for CMV.

 

Option C. Rubella: This is incorrect because Rubella typically presents with other signs such as congenital heart defects, cataracts, and deafness, and does not show owl eye inclusions.

 

Option D. Measles: This is incorrect because Measles does not cause owl eye inclusions and is not associated with hepatosplenomegaly in neonates.

 

Educational objective:

 

Owl eye appearance inclusion bodies in the urine, along with hepatosplenomegaly, in a neonate is highly indicative of congenital CMV infection.

questions.stem: A patient is suffering from a painful vesicular eruption at the T-4 dermatome. The cause is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Herpes zoster

 

Herpes zoster (shingles) is characterized by a painful vesicular rash that is typically confined to a single dermatome, such as the T-4 dermatome, and does not cross the midline of the body. It results from the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), which remains dormant in sensory ganglia after a person has recovered from chickenpox (initial VZV infection).

 

When the immune system is weakened, or in older adults, the virus can reactivate, leading to the appearance of painful vesicular eruptions in the skin area supplied by the affected sensory nerve. The pain, often described as burning or tingling, precedes the appearance of the vesicles and can be quite severe, known as postherpetic neuralgia if it persists after the rash resolves.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. EBV infection: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is associated with infectious mononucleosis and certain cancers, but it does not cause localized vesicular eruptions along a dermatome.

 

Option C. CMV infection: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) can cause various symptoms, particularly in immunocompromised individuals, but it does not typically present as a dermatomal vesicular rash.

 

Option D. Herpes simplex: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) causes painful vesicles, usually around the mouth (HSV-1) or genital area (HSV-2), but it is not associated with the dermatomal pattern of eruption seen in herpes zoster.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Herpes zoster (shingles) presents as a painful vesicular rash restricted to a single dermatome (e.g., T-4) and occurs due to the reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in sensory ganglia. It is distinguished by its unilateral presentation and does not cross the midline.

questions.stem: Which of these need V factor?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) H. paraphrophilus

 

Haemophilus species require different growth factors for cultivation, specifically X (hemin) and V (NAD) factors. 

 

The question asks for a species that requires only V factor:

 

H. paraphrophilus requires only V factor (NAD) for growth.

 

Haemophilus influenzae, H. aegyptius, and H. haemolyticus require both X (hemin) and V (NAD) factors.

 

H. ducreyi requires only X factor for growth.

 

This distinction is important for laboratory identification of different Haemophilus species using media such as chocolate agar, which supplies both X and V factors.

 

Disk test 

 

Species that require X factor, but not V factor → H. ducreyi 

 

Species that require V factor, but not X factor → H. parainfluenzae, 

H. Parahaemolyticus, A. paraphrophilus 

 

Species that require both X and V factors H. influenzae, H. 

aegyptius, H. haemolyticus

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

H. paraphrophilus requires only V factor (NAD) for growth, while other species like H. influenzae and H. aegyptius need both X and V factors.

questions.stem: False About the mechanism of bacterial toxins:

options.label: A
options.text: Cholera toxin acts by inhibition of guanylcyclase

options.label: C
options.text: Shiga toxin act by inhibiting protein synthesis

options.label: D
options.text: Diphtheria toxin act by inhibiting protein synthesis

questions.answerText: Cholera toxin acts by inhibition of guanylcyclase
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Cholera toxin acts by inhibition of guanylcyclase

 

Cholera toxin does not inhibit guanyl cyclase. Instead, it stimulates adenyl cyclase, leading to increased production of cyclic AMP (cAMP). This increase in cAMP causes excessive water and electrolyte secretion, resulting in the watery diarrhea typical of cholera.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Botulinum toxin inhibits Ach release: Correct. Botulinum toxin inhibits the release of acetylcholine (Ach) at the neuromuscular junction. This leads to flaccid paralysis because muscle contractions are blocked, resulting in conditions such as floppy baby syndrome.

 

Option C. Shiga toxin acts by inhibiting protein synthesis: Correct. Shiga toxin, produced by Shigella dysenteriae, inhibits protein synthesis by targeting ribosomes, leading to cell death, especially in the intestines, which results in bloody diarrhea.

 

Option D. Diphtheria toxin acts by inhibiting protein synthesis: Correct. Diphtheria toxin also inhibits protein synthesis by interfering with elongation factor-2 (EF-2), a key factor for protein synthesis. This results in cell death, much like the effect of Shiga toxin, though they affect different targets.

 

Additional Information:

 

Act by inhibiting protein synthesis 

 

DPSS 

 

  • Diphtheria toxin
  • Pseudomonas toxin 
  • Shiga toxin 
  • Shiga like toxin or verotoxin of EHEC

 

Act by increasing cAMP 

 

  • BVEB 
  • Bacillus anthrax
  • Vibrio
  • ETEC
  • Bordetella

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Cholera toxin stimulates adenyl cyclase, leading to increased cAMP.
  • Botulinum toxin inhibits acetylcholine release, resulting in flaccid paralysis.
  • Shiga and Diphtheria toxins inhibit protein synthesis, causing cellular damage

questions.stem: A 30-year-old patient presented with features of acute meningoencephalitis in the casualty. His CSF on wet mount microscopy revealed motile unicellular microorganisms. The most likely organism is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Naegleria fowleri

 

The presentation of acute meningoencephalitis with the presence of motile unicellular organisms in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is highly indicative of Naegleria fowleri. This organism is a free-living amoeba that can cause primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), a rapidly progressing and often fatal condition. N. fowleri is typically acquired through swimming in warm, freshwater bodies, where the amoeba enters the body through the nasal passages, ascends through the cribriform plate, and invades the central nervous system (CNS).

 

The motility observed in the wet mount is due to the trophozoite form of Naegleria fowleri, which has a flagellated stage that can be seen in CSF samples. 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Acanthamoeba castellani: This organism can cause granulomatous amoebic encephalitis (GAE), but it typically presents more slowly and is not acute in nature. It often affects immunocompromised patients, whereas N. fowleri causes a more acute condition.

 

Option C. Entamoeba histolytica: This amoeba primarily causes amebic dysentery and liver abscesses. It does not typically cause meningoencephalitis and would not be found as a motile organism in the CSF.

 

Option D. Trypanosoma cruzi: This protozoan causes Chagas disease, characterized by chronic cardiac and gastrointestinal symptoms. It is not known for causing acute meningoencephalitis with motile trophozoites in the CSF.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Acute meningoencephalitis with motile trophozoites in the CSF is characteristic of Naegleria fowleri, a free-living amoeba that can cause primary amoebic meningoencephalitis.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old boy went for trekking and came back with a history of rash. Weil-Felix test revealed elevated Ox 2 and Ox 19 titers. What is the most likely organism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Rickettsia rickettsii 

 

The Weil-Felix test is a diagnostic tool that detects antibodies to Proteus antigens, which cross-react with antigens of Rickettsial organisms. The interpretation depends on the antigen titer pattern:

 

  • OX19 positive and OX2 positive: Indicates species such as Rickettsia rickettsii (the causative agent of Rocky Mountain spotted fever) and Rickettsia conorii (Mediterranean spotted fever).
  • OXK positive: Indicates Orientia tsutsugamushi (Scrub Typhus).
  • OX19 positive only: Indicates Rickettsia prowazekii (epidemic typhus) or Rickettsia typhi (endemic typhus).

 

In this scenario, a history of trekking suggests an outdoor exposure to ticks, which are vectors for Rickettsia rickettsii. The disease presents with fever, headache, myalgia, and a characteristic rash that begins on the extremities (wrists, ankles) and spreads centrally.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Rickettsia prowazekii: OX19 positive but OX2 negative. It causes epidemic typhus, commonly associated with poor hygiene and body louse infestation rather than trekking.

 

Option C. Rickettsia typhi: OX19 positive but OX2 negative. It causes endemic typhus (murine typhus), typically transmitted by fleas in urban areas rather than outdoor exposure.

 

Option D. Scrub typhus: Caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, which is OXK positive but OX19 and OX2 negative. It is associated with fever, rash, and an eschar at the site of the mite bite, but the Weil-Felix test pattern in this case does not match scrub typhus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

When interpreting the Weil-Felix test for Rickettsial infections:

 

  • OX19 and OX2 positivity indicates Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Rickettsia rickettsii) or Mediterranean spotted fever (Rickettsia conorii).
  • A history of trekking and tick exposure points to Rickettsia rickettsii as the most likely cause.

questions.stem: Reduviid bug is a vector for the transmission of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Chagas disease

 

The Reduviid bug is the vector for the transmission of Chagas disease, which is caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi. The disease is transmitted when the Reduviid bug bites a person and defecates near the wound, introducing the trypomastigote form of the parasite into the bloodstream. The Reduviid bug is also known as the kissing bug. In the initial stages of the disease, there is Romano sign, which is unilateral conjunctivitis caused by inflammation. In later stages, multiple organs can be affected, including the heart (causing cardiomyopathy), the esophagus (leading to megaesophagus), and the colon (leading to megacolon). This distinguishes Chagas disease from other diseases, like African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness), which involves the brain and is transmitted by the tsetse fly.

 

Note:

 

  • Trypanosoma cruzi and Trypanosoma brucei are both haemoflagellates but have different vectors.
    • Trypanosoma brucei → Vector: tsetse fly
    • Trypanosoma cruzi → Vector: Rudovic bug
  • Mode of transmission:
    • Trypanosoma brucei: Transmission via saliva (tripomastigotes enter blood).
    • Trypanosoma cruzi: Transmission via feces of the Rudovic bug (tripomastigotes enter blood).
  • Signs in early stage:
    • Trypanosoma brucei → Winterbottom sign (posterior cervical lymphadenopathy).
    • Trypanosoma cruzi → Romano sign (unilateral conjunctivitis).
  • Late-stage involvement:
    • Trypanosoma brucei → Affects the brain, leading to sleeping sickness.
    • Trypanosoma cruzi → Affects three organs:
      • Heart → Cardiomyopathy.
      • Esophagus → Megaesophagus.
      • Colon → Megacolon.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Relapsing fever: This is incorrect because Relapsing fever is transmitted by lice or ticks, not the Reduviid bug.

 

Option B. Lyme’s disease: This is incorrect because Lyme disease is transmitted by the Ixodes tick, not the Reduviid bug.

 

Option C. Scrub typhus: This is incorrect because Scrub typhus is transmitted by mites (chiggers), not the Reduviid bug.

 

Educational objective:

 

The Reduviid bug is the vector for Chagas disease, which is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi and can lead to significant heart, esophagus, and colon damage in later stages.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old male had unprotected sexual intercourse with a commercial sex worker. Two weeks later, he developed a painless, indurated ulcer on the glans that exuded clear serum on pressure. Inguinal lymph nodes in both groins were enlarged and not tender. The most appropriate diagnostic test is:

options.label: B
options.text: Dark field microscopy of ulcer discharge

options.label: C
options.text: Giemsa stain of lymph node aspirate

questions.answerText: Dark field microscopy of ulcer discharge
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Dark field microscopy of ulcer discharge

 

The clinical presentation of a painless, indurated ulcer on the genitalia, along with enlarged, non-tender inguinal lymph nodes, is characteristic of primary syphilis. Syphilis is caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum. The most appropriate diagnostic test for primary syphilis is dark field microscopy of the ulcer discharge. This method allows for the direct visualization of Treponema pallidum, which appears as spiral-shaped organisms exhibiting characteristic corkscrew motility.

 

 

 

Dark field microscopy is particularly useful in the early stage of syphilis, where serological tests may still be negative. It provides a definitive diagnosis by directly identifying the causative organism.

 

Other Option:

 

Option A. Gram’s stain of ulcer discharge: Treponema pallidum is not visualized well with Gram staining due to its thin and delicate structure. Therefore, Gram’s stain is not appropriate for diagnosing syphilis.

 

Option C. Giemsa stain of lymph node aspirate: Giemsa stain is used for detecting certain intracellular organisms like Leishmania or Plasmodium, but it is not suitable for detecting Treponema pallidum.

 

Option D. ELISA for HIV infection: While HIV testing is recommended in patients with sexually transmitted infections, it is not the primary diagnostic test for the ulcer in this case. The presentation is specific to primary syphilis, making dark field microscopy the appropriate choice.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In a patient with a painless, indurated ulcer on the genitalia and enlarged, non-tender lymph nodes, dark field microscopy is the best initial diagnostic test for detecting Treponema pallidum in primary syphilis.




ore, Gram’s stain is not appropriate for diagnosing syphilis. Option C. Giemsa stain of lymph node aspirate: Giemsa stain is used for detecting certain intracellular organisms like Leishmania or Plasmodium, but it is not suitable for detecting Treponema pallidum. Option D. ELISA for HIV infection: While HIV testing is recommended in patients with sexually transmitted infections, it is not the primary diagnostic test for the ulcer in this case. The presentation is specific to primary syphilis, making dark field microscopy the appropriate choice. Educational Objective: In a patient with a painless, indurated ulcer on the genitalia and enlarged, non-tender lymph nodes, dark field microscopy is the best initial diagnostic test for detecting Treponema pallidum in primary syphilis.

questions.stem: A child with 3 years of age presents with weakness with Hb level <5 g/dL. History of blood loss in stool was present. What would be the causative organism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Hookworm

 

Hookworms are a common cause of chronic intestinal blood loss, which can lead to iron deficiency anemia, particularly in children. The two species of hookworms, Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale, attach themselves to the intestinal walls, causing blood loss through their feeding process. This loss can become significant over time, leading to severe anemia, as seen in this child with a hemoglobin level of less than 5 g/dL. The presence of blood loss in the stool is a hallmark sign of hookworm infection, supporting the diagnosis in this case.

 

 

Ancylostoma and Necator

 

Contains a segmented ovum with four blastomeres

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Roundworm: Roundworms (Ascaris lumbricoides) typically do not cause significant blood loss or anemia. They cause problems such as malnutrition or intestinal obstruction due to their large size but are not associated with chronic bleeding.

 

Option C. Whipworm: Whipworm (Trichuris trichiura) can cause some blood loss but not to the extent of causing severe anemia, as is evident in this case. Whipworm infections are generally associated with chronic diarrhea rather than significant blood loss.

 

Option D. Pinworm: Pinworms (Enterobius vermicularis) are primarily associated with perianal itching and do not cause intestinal blood loss or anemia. They are not capable of causing the severe anemia seen in this scenario.

 

Additional information:

 

Pernicious anemia:

 

  • Caused by Diphyllobothrium latum (a fish tapeworm).
  • This parasite absorbs large amounts of vitamin B12 from the host, leading to vitamin B12 deficiency and pernicious anemia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hookworms, specifically Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale, cause chronic intestinal blood loss leading to iron deficiency anemia, especially in children.

questions.stem: Neil Mooser reaction or tunica reaction is useful to differentiate between:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) R. prowazekii and R. typhi

 

The Neil Mooser reaction (also called the tunica reaction) is used to differentiate between epidemic typhus, caused by Rickettsia prowazekii, and endemic typhus, caused by Rickettsia typhi. In this reaction, the test is performed on a male guinea pig by injecting the suspected pathogen into the scrotum. If the scrotum swells, the test is positive, indicating R. typhi (endemic typhus). If there is no swelling, the test is negative, indicating R. prowazekii (epidemic typhus).

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. R. typhi and R. rickettsia: Incorrect. The Neil Mooser reaction is not used to differentiate R. typhi from R. rickettsia.

 

Option C. R. prowazekii and R. rickettsia: Incorrect. The test is specific for distinguishing R. prowazekii from R. typhi.

 

Option D. R. rickettsia and C. burnetti: Incorrect. The Neil Mooser reaction does not differentiate between R. rickettsia and C. burnetti.

 

Educational objective:

 

The Neil Mooser reaction differentiates Rickettsia prowazekii (epidemic typhus, negative reaction) from Rickettsia typhi (endemic typhus, positive reaction).

questions.stem: Which of the following egg contains three pairs of hooklets and polar filaments but is bile nonstained?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) H. nana

 

Hymenolepis nana (H. nana) is a dwarf tapeworm, and its eggs have specific characteristics that differentiate it from others:

 

The egg contains an oncosphere with three pairs of hooklets.

 

The egg is bile nonstained (i.e., it does not absorb bile pigments, making it colorless).

 

It has polar filaments that emerge from the poles and lie between the two membranes.

 

The egg serves both as the infective form and the diagnostic form of the parasite.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. T. solium: Incorrect. Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) eggs do not have polar filaments and are bile-stained.

 

Option C. T. saginata: Incorrect. Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm) eggs are also bile-stained and lack polar filaments.

 

Option D. E. granulosus: Incorrect. Echinococcus granulosus eggs are bile-stained, not bile nonstained, and do not have polar filaments.

 

Note:

 

Bile non-stained (B negative):

 

Mnemonic "NEHA" for bile-negative eggs:

 

  • N: Necator americanus
  • E: Enterobius vermicularis 
  • H: Hymenolepis nana
  • A: Ancylostoma duodenale

 

Educational objective:

 

H. nana eggs are characterized by being bile nonstained, containing three pairs of hooklets, and having polar filaments,

questions.stemHtml: A 33-year-old sexually active male is experiencing urethral discharge for the past 8 months, along with a burning sensation during urination. A Gram-stained smear of a urethral swab sample is shown below:The causative organism is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Neisseria gonorrhoeae

 

The image provided shows Gram-negative cocci arranged in pairs (diplococci) with a characteristic kidney or coffee-bean shape. These cocci are observed within the cytoplasm of neutrophils, indicating an intracellular nature. This presentation is highly indicative of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a common cause of sexually transmitted urethritis in men.

 

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is known for causing symptoms such as urethral discharge and dysuria (painful urination). The Gram stain showing intracellular Gram-negative diplococci in neutrophils is a hallmark of gonococcal infection, distinguishing it from other potential causes of urethritis.

 

 

 

N. Meningitidis 

Diplococci 

Half moon shaped 

One capsule around each pair → 12 types 

(A, B, C, X, Y,Z, W-135, 29E, H, I, K, L) 

 

 

N. Gonorrhoeae 

Diplococci 

Kidney bean shaped 

No capsule

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Chlamydia trachomatis: This organism can also cause urethritis, but it is not visible on a Gram stain since it lacks a typical cell wall. Chlamydia is better detected using nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT).

 

Option C. Mycoplasma hominis: This organism lacks a cell wall and would not appear on Gram staining. It is associated with various genitourinary infections but is not a common cause of purulent urethritis like N. gonorrhoeae.

 

Option D. Ureaplasma urealyticum: Similar to Mycoplasma, it lacks a cell wall and would not be detected on a Gram stain. It is a cause of non-gonococcal urethritis, but the Gram-negative diplococci seen here rule it out.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of Gram-negative, intracellular diplococci in a urethral swab from a patient with urethritis is characteristic of Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

questions.stemHtml: A patient with benign hypertrophy of the prostate (BPH) was admitted to the hospital for 3 weeks. He subsequently developed a suspected catheter-associated urinary tract infection (UTI). The tip of the catheter was sent for culture, and the growth was observed on blood agar. After 24 hours, the blood agar showed the following appearance. What is the likely causative agent for the UTI?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Proteus mirabilis

 

The image of the blood agar shows a characteristic swarming motility, which is highly suggestive of Proteus mirabilis. Proteus species, particularly P. mirabilis, are known to cause catheter-associated urinary tract infections (UTIs), especially in patients with conditions like benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), which can cause urine retention. The swarming appearance is due to the ability of Proteus to move rapidly across the surface of the agar, creating a characteristic concentric pattern.

 

Types of Motility 

 

  • Darting    - V. cholera, Campylobactor 
  • Tumbling                        - Listeria at 25°C 
  • Cork screw  - T. pallidum 
  • Swarming    - P. mirabilis, P. vulgaris, Cl. tetani, Bacillus cereus 
  • Lashing        - Borrelia 
  • Stately       - Clostridia 
  • Gliding         -Mycoplasma

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Pseudomonas: While Pseudomonas aeruginosa can cause catheter-associated UTIs, it does not exhibit the swarming motility seen on blood agar. Instead, it forms colonies with a distinctive greenish pigment.

 

Option C. Escherichia coli: E. coli is a common cause of UTIs, especially community-acquired ones. However, it does not display swarming motility on agar; its colonies are typically smooth and non-motile.

 

Option D. Klebsiella pneumoniae: This organism can cause UTIs, particularly in hospitalized patients, but it forms mucoid colonies rather than exhibiting swarming motility.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Swarming motility observed on blood agar is characteristic of Proteus mirabilis, a common cause of catheter-associated UTIs.

questions.stem: All statements are true about mycetoma except:

options.label: B
options.text: Surgery is important component of treatment

options.label: D
options.text: Diagnosis can be made by examination of lesion

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Eumycetoma is caused by bacteria

 

Mycetoma is a chronic granulomatous infection that can be caused by fungi (eumycetoma) or by bacteria (actinomycetoma). The key point here is that eumycetoma is caused by fungi, not bacteria, making option (a) incorrect. The fungi involved in eumycetoma typically include species like Madurella and Scedosporium. In contrast, actinomycetoma is caused by certain bacteria, such as Nocardia and Actinomadura.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Surgery is an important component of treatment: This is true. The treatment for mycetoma often involves surgical removal of the lesion, especially in cases where the infection is advanced or unresponsive to medication. Surgery is followed by antifungal or antibacterial therapy depending on the type of mycetoma.

 

Option C. Usually painless: This is true. Mycetoma often presents as a slowly progressive, painless swelling with multiple sinuses that discharge pus and grains, which are characteristic of the infection.

 

Option D. Diagnosis can be made by examination of lesion: This is true. The diagnosis of mycetoma is often made based on the clinical examination, recognizing the presence of swelling, sinuses, and grains in the discharge. Additional tests like microscopy and culture are used to identify the causative agent.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Eumycetoma is caused by fungi, not bacteria, distinguishing it from actinomycetoma, which is bacterial. Treatment of mycetoma typically involves surgical intervention and is generally painless despite the chronic nature of the disease.

questions.stemHtml: A patient presented with complaints of dysphagia. On UGI Endoscopy, a diagnosis of esophageal candidiasis was made. The organism obtained from the sample was cultured on a specialized media, and the finding shown in the image was visible on microscopy of the culture. What phenomenon is shown below?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Germ tube formation

 

The image demonstrates germ tube formation, also known as the Reynolds Braude phenomenon, which is a key feature used to differentiate Candida albicans (and C. dubliniensis) from other Candida species. The germ tube test is performed by incubating Candida in human or sheep serum for about 2 hours. After incubation, a wet mount preparation is examined under the microscope to observe the formation of germ tubes, which are tube-like projections extending from the yeast cells. These projections differentiate Candida albicans, which is germ tube positive, from other Candida species, which are germ tube negative.

The germ tube is distinguished from pseudohyphae because it does not have a constriction at its origin, which is characteristic of pseudohyphae.

 

 

  • Additional tests for identifying Candida species include:
    • Dalmau plate technique.
    • ChromAgar (used to differentiate Candida species based on colony color).

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Spore formation: This is incorrect. The image does not show spore formation.

 

Option C. Mould to yeast formation: This is incorrect. The image is showing germ tube formation, not the transition from mould to yeast.

 

Option D. Budding: This is incorrect. Budding involves the formation of a daughter cell from the yeast, but the image depicts germ tube formation.

 

Educational objective:

 

Germ tube formation is a characteristic of Candida albicans and C. dubliniensis, and is identified by tube-like projections extending from yeast cells after incubation in serum, without constrictions at the origin.

questions.stem: True about Botulinum toxin:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Interfere with cholinergic transmission

 

Botulinum toxin interferes with cholinergic transmission by inhibiting the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ), peripheral ganglia, and parasympathetic nerve endings. This inhibition occurs because the toxin blocks the synaptic vesicles from releasing acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft, which is crucial for muscle contraction. As a result, muscles cannot contract, leading to flaccid paralysis—a hallmark of botulism. This mechanism is also the reason why botulinum toxin is used in clinical settings to treat conditions involving muscle spasticity.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Interfere with adrenergic transmission: Botulinum toxin does not affect adrenergic transmission, which involves the release of neurotransmitters like norepinephrine in the sympathetic nervous system.

 

Option C. Increase release of synaptic vesicles: This is incorrect. Botulinum toxin decreases the release of synaptic vesicles containing acetylcholine, leading to reduced muscle activity.

 

Option D. Act also on CNS: Botulinum toxin does not cross the blood-brain barrier and therefore has no direct action on the central nervous system (CNS). Its effects are limited to the peripheral nervous system.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Botulinum toxin works by blocking the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, leading to flaccid paralysis. It specifically interferes with cholinergic transmission but has no effect on the CNS.




ore has no direct action on the central nervous system (CNS). Its effects are limited to the peripheral nervous system. Educational Objective: Botulinum toxin works by blocking the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, leading to flaccid paralysis. It specifically interferes with cholinergic transmission but has no effect on the CNS.

questions.stem: EBV receptors is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) CD 21

 

The Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) uses CD21 (also known as CR2) as its receptor. CD21 is found on B cells and pharyngeal epithelial cells. EBV, also known as the "kissing virus," is transmitted through saliva. After transmission, it enters the B lymphocytes present in the tonsils by binding to the CD21 receptor on these cells. This binding allows the virus to infect the B cells. Once inside the cell, EBV has oncogenic potential, meaning it can lead to the development of cancers such as Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin's lymphoma, and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. In some cases, EBV infection causes infectious mononucleosis, which presents as tonsillitis and is detected using the Paul Bunnell test, also known as the heterophile antibody test.

 

Flow chart:

 

 

Note:

 

  • EBV is an oncogenic virus that can transform cells into cancerous cells.
  • Cancers associated with EBV infection:
  1. Burkitt lymphoma
  2. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
  3. Hodgkin's lymphoma (especially the mixed-cellularity type).
  4. Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. CD 9: This is incorrect because CD9 is not a receptor for EBV.

 

Option C. CD 10: This is incorrect. CD10 is associated with certain leukemias, not EBV entry.

 

Option D. CD 8: This is incorrect because CD8 is a marker for cytotoxic T cells and is not the receptor used by EBV.

 

Educational objective:

 

The CD21 receptor is essential for the entry of EBV into B cells and pharyngeal epithelial cells, leading to infections such as infectious mononucleosis and certain cancers.

questions.stem: All are Koch’s postulates except:

options.label: A
options.text: A microorganism should be constantly associated with the lesions of the disease

options.label: B
options.text: It should be possible to isolate the bacterium in pure culture from the lesions

options.label: C
options.text: Inoculation of such pure culture into laboratory animals should reproduce the lesions

options.label: D
options.text: Administration of broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent dependably eradicates the organisms and cures the diseases

questions.answerText: Administration of broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent dependably eradicates the organisms and cures the diseases
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Administration of broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent dependably eradicates the organisms and cures the diseases

 

The administration of broad-spectrum antimicrobial agents is not one of Koch's postulates. Koch’s postulates are a set of principles developed to establish the link between a microorganism and a disease. They require the following:

 

  1. The microorganism should be found in all individuals suffering from the disease and not in healthy individuals.
  2. The microorganism should be isolated from a diseased organism and grown in pure culture.
  3. When this pure culture is introduced into a healthy, susceptible organism, it should cause the same disease.
  4. The microorganism should then be re-isolated from the experimentally infected organism and identified as being identical to the original specific causative agent.

 

 

Note: 

 

 Microorganisms not meeting the criteria of koch's postulates are:

 

  • M. leprae 
  • T. pallidum 
  • N. gonorrhoeae 

 

Educational objective:

 

Koch's postulates outline the criteria for establishing a causative relationship between a microorganism and a disease, but antimicrobial treatment is not one of these postulates.

questions.stem: Eggs of which of the following parasites cause intense pruritus in the perianal skin:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Enterobius vermicularis

 

Enterobius vermicularis, commonly known as pinworm, is the causative agent of intense perianal itching, especially in children. The pruritus (itching) is most pronounced at night, a condition referred to as nocturnal pruritus. This occurs because the female pinworm migrates to the perianal area during the night to lay eggs, causing irritation and itching. The eggs are sticky, which further contributes to the discomfort. This characteristic nocturnal itching helps differentiate E. vermicularis infection from other parasitic infections.

 

Egg 

 

Planoconvex in shape i.e., flattened on the ventral side and convex on the dorsal side. 

 

 

Surrounded by a transparent shell

Contains a tadpole-like larva. 

Colourless i.e., Not bile-stained.

Floats in saturated solution of common salt.

 

MOT → Ingestion of eggs contaminated with fingers due to inadequate hand washing or nail biting habit

 

 

Infective form 

 

Eggs

 

Host → 1 

 

  • Definitive host → Man
  • Intermediate host → Nil

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ascaris: Ascaris lumbricoides causes ascariasis, which generally affects the intestines and lungs but does not cause intense perianal itching.

 

Option B. Hookworm: Hookworm infections typically result in symptoms like anemia and gastrointestinal distress due to blood loss but do not cause pruritus in the perianal region.

 

Option D. Trichuris: Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) can cause gastrointestinal symptoms like diarrhea and abdominal pain but is not associated with perianal itching.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Intense nocturnal pruritus in the perianal region is a classic symptom of Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) infection, especially in children.
