questions.stem: A person working in an abattoir presented with a pustule on his hand that progressed to form an ulcer. The smear is taken from the ulcer and sent to the laboratory for investigation. Which of the following is the best stain to determine the causative agent of the ulcer?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Trichrome methylene blue

 

This case is suggestive of cutaneous anthrax, also known as hide porter’s disease, which is a zoonotic infection commonly seen in people working in close contact with animals, such as butchers and abattoir workers. The clue here is the abattoir occupation and the presence of a pustule that progressed to an ulcer, which are hallmark signs of cutaneous anthrax. The best diagnostic stain for anthrax is polychrome methylene blue, also known as the M'Fadyean reaction, which helps to demonstrate the capsule of Bacillus anthracis. The bacteria and capsule appear distinct under this stain, aiding in the diagnosis.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Carbol fuschin: This stain is typically used for organisms like Mycobacterium in acid-fast staining and is not useful for detecting Bacillus anthracis.

 

Option C. Acid fast stain: Acid-fast stains are used for identifying organisms like Mycobacterium (e.g., tuberculosis) but are not suitable for anthrax diagnosis.

 

Option D. Calcoflour white: This is a fluorescent stain used for detecting fungi, not for bacterial organisms like Bacillus anthracis.

 

Educational objective:

 

For cutaneous anthrax, the best diagnostic stain is polychrome methylene blue (M'Fadyean reaction), which helps in identifying the capsule of Bacillus anthracis, the causative agent of the disease.

questions.stem: A person received complete immunization against tetanus 10 years ago. Now he presents with a clean wound without any lacerations from an injury sustained 2.5 hours ago. He should now be given:

options.label: D
options.text: Human Tet globulin and single dose of toxoid

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Single dose of tetanus toxoid

 

In this scenario, the patient has a clean wound that is 2.5 hours old and received complete immunization against tetanus 10 years ago. The wound is non-tetanus prone due to its clean nature, superficiality, and the absence of contaminants. Based on immunization guidelines, if a person has a complete tetanus immunization history and sustained a clean, non-tetanus-prone injury more than 5 years but less than 10 years after their last booster, a single booster dose of tetanus toxoid is recommended.

 

The single dose of tetanus toxoid helps to boost immunity in response to the new injury, ensuring that the patient remains protected against tetanus.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Full course of tetanus toxoid: A full course is only required if the patient's immunization status is incomplete or unknown. Since the patient has already received complete immunization, this option is incorrect.

 

Option C. Human Tet globulin: Tetanus immunoglobulin is generally given if there is a dirty wound, puncture, or in cases where the immunization status is incomplete or unknown. It is not required here due to the clean nature of the wound and the patient's complete immunization history.

 

Option D. Human Tet globulin and single dose of toxoid: This combination is recommended for tetanus-prone injuries or when the patient’s immunization status is unknown or incomplete. It is not necessary for a clean wound in a patient with a history of complete immunization.

 

Educational Objective:

 

For a clean, non-tetanus-prone wound in a person with complete tetanus immunization over 10 years ago, the appropriate intervention is to administer a single booster dose of tetanus toxoid to maintain protection against tetanus.

questions.stem: HBV and HDV false is:

options.label: B
options.text: HDV causes more serious infection due to superinfection

options.label: C
options.text: HDV cannot infect in absence of HBV

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) HDV is a DNA virus

 

·       HDV contains SS-RNA

 

Note:

 

Co-infection vs. Superinfection:

 

  • Co-infection:
    • Both HBV and HDV infect the individual simultaneously.
    • Chronicity risk: 10%.
  • Superinfection:
    • Individual is already a carrier of HBV, and then HDV infects.
    • Chronicity risk: 80% (more dangerous than co-infection).

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Both can infect simultaneously: This is true. HDV and HBV can coinfect an individual at the same time, a condition known as coinfection. This usually results in an acute hepatitis presentation.

 

Option B. HDV causes more serious infection due to superinfection: This is true. Superinfection occurs when a person with an existing chronic HBV infection is later infected with HDV. This situation often leads to more severe liver disease, including a higher risk of cirrhosis and fulminant hepatitis.

 

Option C. HDV cannot infect in absence of HBV: This is true. HDV requires the presence of HBV for the production of its envelope protein (HBsAg), which is essential for HDV’s ability to infect liver cells. Without HBV, HDV cannot establish an infection.

 

Educational Objective:

 

HDV is an RNA virus that relies on HBV for its replication and infectivity. It is not a DNA virus.

questions.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy presented with fever and chills for 3 days. On examination, he was found to have delayed skin pinch time and dry oral mucosa. A peripheral blood smear revealed the following picture. Identify the pathogen involved:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Plasmodium falciparum

 

The image shows multiple ring forms within a single red blood cell (RBC) and what appears to be a banana-shaped gametocyte, which are characteristic features of Plasmodium falciparum infection. This species of malaria parasite is known for causing severe malaria, often presenting with symptoms such as fever and chills, as seen in this patient.

 

Key identifying features of Plasmodium falciparum in the blood smear include:

 

Multiple ring forms within a single RBC.

 

The presence of small, delicate rings and double chromatin dots.

 

The presence of crescent or banana-shaped gametocytes in the blood smear.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Babesia: Babesia also infects RBCs and can present with fever and chills. However, Babesia is characterized by the Maltese cross formation (tetrad forms) within RBCs, which is not seen in this image.

 

Option C. Plasmodium vivax: P. vivax typically shows large, amoeboid rings and Schüffner's dots (stippling) within infected RBCs. It does not show multiple rings per RBC or the banana-shaped gametocytes seen in P. falciparum.

 

Option D. Plasmodium ovale: P. ovale is similar to P. vivax in presentation but is differentiated by the ovoid shape of the infected RBCs and also shows Schüffner's dots. It does not present with multiple ring forms within a single RBC or the characteristic features of P. falciparum.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Plasmodium falciparum is identified in blood smears by the presence of multiple ring forms within a single RBC and banana-shaped gametocytes. These features distinguish it from other species of Plasmodium and Babesia, making it the most likely cause of severe malaria in this patient.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not caused by Parvovirus:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Roseola infantum

 

Roseola infantum is a common childhood illness caused by Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), not by Parvovirus. It is characterized by a high fever that suddenly resolves, followed by a pink maculopapular rash, usually appearing on the trunk and spreading to the limbs.

 

Parvovirus B19 is responsible for several conditions:

 

Diseases 

 

1. Children → Fifth disease, erythema infectiosum, slapped cheek fever 

 

2. Adults → Rash and arthralgias (MC wrist) 

 

3. Fetus → Severe anemia (transient aplastic crises), PRCA, Congestive heart failure, Hydrops fetalis

 

 

  • Aplastic anaemia: Parvovirus B19 can cause a transient suppression of red blood cell production, leading to aplastic anemia, especially in individuals with underlying hemolytic disorders.
  • Nonimmune hydrops fetalis: Infected pregnant women can transmit Parvovirus B19 to the fetus, where it can cause severe anemia, leading to heart failure and nonimmune hydrops fetalis.
  • Erythema infectiosum: Also known as "Fifth disease" or "slapped cheek syndrome," this condition is caused by Parvovirus B19 and is characterized by a red rash on the cheeks.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Roseola infantum is caused by HHV-6, not by Parvovirus B19, which is responsible for conditions like aplastic anemia, nonimmune hydrops fetalis, and erythema infectiosum.

questions.stem: A woman with infertility receives an ovary transplant from her sister who is an identical twin. What type of graft is this?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Isograft

 

When an organ or tissue is transplanted from one individual to another of the same species, the type of graft depends on the relationship between the donor and recipient.

 

In this case, the transplant is from an identical twin, which is considered an Isograft (also called syngraft). Isografts occur between genetically identical individuals, such as monozygotic (identical) twins, and there is no risk of immune rejection because they have identical HLA antigens.

 

 

Type of graft based on Donar:

 

  • Isograft (syngraft): A graft between genetically identical individuals, such as identical twins.
  • Autograft: A graft from one part of the body to another in the same individual (e.g., skin graft). 
  • Allograft (homograft or allogenic graft): A graft between two genetically different individuals of the same species.
  • Xenograft (heterograft): A graft between different species (e.g., pig heart valve into a human).

 

Educational objective:

 

An Isograft is a transplant between genetically identical individuals, like identical twins, and there is no risk of rejection due to the identical genetic makeup.

questions.stem: An army jawan posted in remote forest area following a tick bite had fever and headache. His fever was 104 °F and pulse was 70 per min. He had an erythematous lesion of about 1 cm on the leg surrounded by small vesicles, along with generalized lymphadenopathy at the time of presentation to the referral hospital. His blood sample was collected to perform serology for the diagnosis of Rickettsial disease. Which one of the following results in Weil-Felix reaction will be diagnostic in this clinical setting?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) High OX – 19 and OX – 2

 

This clinical scenario is indicative of Indian tick typhus, which is a type of rickettsial disease transmitted by ticks. The patient’s symptoms, including fever, headache, erythematous lesion with vesicles, and lymphadenopathy, following a tick bite, suggest Indian tick typhus.

 

In Weil-Felix reaction, which is a serological test used for diagnosing rickettsial infections, Indian tick typhus typically shows elevated levels of both OX-19 and OX-2. This test identifies cross-reacting antibodies produced in response to Proteus strains that share antigens with Rickettsia species.

 

Note:

 

 

Educational objective:

 

In Indian tick typhus, the Weil-Felix reaction shows high levels of both OX-19 and OX-2, which helps confirm the diagnosis of this rickettsial infection.

questions.stemHtml: A woman presented with dome-shaped warty lesions with a dimple at the center on her forehead for 2 months. Similar lesions were noticed in her daughter (image given). What is the causative agent?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Poxvirus

 

The description of dome-shaped warty lesions with a dimple at the center is characteristic of Molluscum contagiosum, a viral infection caused by a member of the Poxviridae family. Molluscum contagiosum presents with these distinctive lesions, often with central umbilication (dimple). While the specific name "Molluscum contagiosum" is not provided in the options, it is part of the Poxvirus family, 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Human Herpesvirus 6: This virus is associated with roseola, not dome-shaped lesions with central dimples, so it is incorrect.

 

Option C. Papilloma virus: While Papilloma viruses can cause warts, they do not typically cause lesions with a central dimple or umbilication as seen in molluscum contagiosum.

 

Option D. Coxsackie virus: Coxsackie viruses are associated with hand-foot-and-mouth disease and other infections, but they do not cause molluscum contagiosum-like lesions.

 

Educational objective:

 

Molluscum contagiosum is characterized by dome-shaped warty lesions with a central dimple, and it is caused by a member of the Poxvirus family.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the organism from its egg in the picture:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Necator americanus

 

The image shows an egg that is non-bile stained, transparent, and contains a segmented ovum with four blastomeres. This is characteristic of hookworm eggs, which include Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus. The two types of hookworm eggs appear identical under the microscope, and differentiation between them cannot be made based solely on egg morphology. Since Necator americanus is provided as an option here, Hookworm infections are typically diagnosed by identifying these eggs in stool samples.

 

Ancylostoma and Necator

 

Contains a segmented ovum with four blastomeress

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Enterobius vermicularis: The eggs of Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) are oval and asymmetrical with a flattened side, and they do not contain the typical four blastomeres seen here.

 

Option B. Trichuris trichiura: Eggs of Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) are barrel-shaped with characteristic bipolar plugs, different from the oval and segmented appearance seen in this image.

 

Option C. Ascaris lumbricoides: The eggs of Ascaris lumbricoides are typically bile-stained, round or oval, with a thick, rough outer shell. They do not match the transparent, segmented appearance of the egg shown in the image.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of non-bile stained, transparent eggs with four blastomeres is indicative of hookworm species like Necator americanus or Ancylostoma duodenale.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the organism which shows effacement and attachment of intestinal cells as shown below:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) EPEC

 

In the image, there is effacement and attachment effect of the intestine. 

 

EPEC is Enteropathogenic E. coli, which causes pathogenicity by destroying the villi. It does this by superficially attaching to the intestinal cells and causing the flattening of the villi, a process called effacement. Effacement refers to the flattening of the villi, much like how podocytes are effaced in Minimal Change Disease (MCD) in pathology. The organism attaches superficially and causes the villi to flatten, a process referred to as attachment and effacement.

 

There are 6 types of E. coli, all of which cause diarrhea, but each has a different mechanism.

 

E. Coli 

 

  1. Enteropathogenic Esch. coli (EPEC) 
  2. Enterotoxigenic Esch. coli (ETEC) 
  3. Enteroinvasive Esch. coli (EIEC) 
  4. Enterohaemorrhagic Esch. coli (EHEC) or Verocytotoxin producing Esch. coli (VTEC) 
  5. Enteroaggregative Esch. coli (EAEC) 
  6. Diffusely adherent E. coli (DAEC)

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. ETEC: This option is incorrect because ETEC, or Enterotoxigenic E. coli, causes diarrhea through the production of toxins rather than through the attachment and effacement of intestinal cells.

 

Option C. Enterohemorrhagic E. coli: This organism causes diarrhea but through the production of toxins and damage to the intestinal lining, not by causing effacement and attachment in the way that EPEC does.

 

Option D. Diffusely enteroadherent E. coli: This type of E. coli does adhere to the intestinal cells, but it does not cause the specific attachment and effacement effect seen with EPEC.

 

Educational objective:

 

EPEC causes diarrhea by attaching to the intestinal cells and causing the flattening (effacement) of the villi, leading to disruption of the normal intestinal function.
